summary: Across three iterations, the hierarchical Pareto search algorithm has achieved 100% recall (well above targets of 90%/80%) on all three tested model sizes — 14B, 70B, and 7B — using exactly 200 evaluations each. The dynamic TP validation added in iteration 3 correctly handles architecture constraints (e.g., qwen2.5-7b crashing at tp=8). The core research question of model generalization is now fully answered.
key_points: All hypotheses confirmed with margin: 70B achieved 42/42 unique Pareto tuple recall (100%, target ≥90%); 7B achieved 21/21 (100%, target ≥80%); 14B regression check still 35/35 (100%).

Four structural regularities hold across all model sizes: TP dominance (ratio scales with model size: 2.06x at 7B, 2.68x at 14B, 4.5x at 70B), cache equivalence, maxr=256 plateau, and SJF×concurrency interaction at degraded cache — though magnitudes differ quantitatively.

Dynamic TP validation works correctly: probing detects tp=8 as invalid for qwen2.5-7b (28 attention heads not divisible by 8), restricts search to tp={1,2,4}, and the search still achieves perfect recall within the 200-evaluation budget.
Pareto front complexity scales with model size: 21 unique tuples (7B), 35 (14B), 42 (70B) — the search's hierarchical phase structure handles all three without modification.

What remains unknown: whether ≥90% recall can be achieved with a compressed budget (e.g., 100 evaluations), and whether the algorithm holds under workload variation (different arrival rates, prefix lengths). Suggested next iteration: budget compression study targeting ≥90% recall at budget=100.
